title: For Enemies
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 16 of 40
content:
The Ministry wanted a complete list of every spell Snape had invented.

Snape wanted the Ministry to go to hell.

I considered both positions understandable.

The request arrived by owl on a Tuesday morning in a cream envelope stamped with the Department of Magical Law Enforcement seal. Snape read it once, folded it into quarters, and placed it beneath a jar of flobberworm mucus.

“That is not technically a response,” I said.

“It has been filed.”

“Under biological waste?”

“Appropriately.”

I moved the jar before the letter absorbed anything unpleasant.

“The hearing is in two weeks. Ignoring them seems strategically unwise.”

“So does providing the Ministry with a convenient catalogue of my private research.”

“They already know about Sectumsempra, Levicorpus, Liberacorpus, Langlock, and Muffliato.”

His eyes narrowed.

“You have been studying.”

“I have access to newspapers.”

“A regrettable condition.”

“And Harry's testimony is public.”

“An even more regrettable condition.”

I opened the letter.

“They're asking for spells with possible evidentiary relevance.”

“They are asking for everything and hoping I am too tired to object.”

I reread the language.

He was right.

That annoyed me.

“Fine,” I said. “We answer narrowly.”

“We answer nothing.”

“Do you want them assuming every undocumented spell is Dark magic?”

“They do already.”

“Do you want that assumption in the hearing record?”

His jaw tightened.

We had been preparing for the hearing in pieces. Evidence boxes. Statements. Potion analyses. Letters from former students, some condemning him and some describing things he had done during the last year to protect them. Harry Potter had agreed to testify. McGonagall had agreed to testify. Several members of the Order had opinions so complicated they required appendices.

Snape treated the process like a second war.

Every request was a possible trap.

Every friendly letter contained an angle.

Every compliment made him suspicious.

I understood why.

I was also tired of it.

“Let's make our own categories,” I said.

His eyebrow rose.

“Harmless utility. Defensive. Offensive but nonlethal. Dangerous. Dark.”

“Childish.”

“Functional.”

“Those categories overlap.”

“Then add notes.”

“You are attempting to reduce spellcraft to a filing cabinet.”

“You love filing cabinets when they're in your house.”

His eyes flashed.

I smiled.

That argument still amused me.

At last he sat.

“Fine.”

I took out a fresh sheet.

“Muffliato.”

“Utility.”

“Privacy.”

“Utility.”

“Potentially useful for espionage.”

“By that standard, doors are Dark objects.”

“Fair. Utility.”

I wrote.

“Langlock.”

“Nonlethal offensive.”

“Also useful during staff meetings?”

He stared.

I wrote nonlethal offensive.

“Levicorpus.”

His face changed.

“Offensive.”

“Nonlethal?”

“Usually.”

“That usually is doing a lot of work.”

“Any jinx can become dangerous in the presence of stairs, cliffs, water, sharp objects, unstable ceilings, or idiots.”

“So Hogwarts.”

“Precisely.”

I wrote the note.

“Sectumsempra.”

“Dangerous. Dark-adjacent, depending on definition.”

“Not simply Dark?”

His gaze sharpened.

“You want honesty or a slogan?”

“Honesty.”

“Dark magic is not a tidy legal species. Some spells are classified by intent, some by mechanism, some by tradition, some because the Ministry wishes to appear decisive. Sectumsempra causes severe physical injury through magical laceration. It was designed for violence. Call it Dark if the form pleases you.”

“What do you call it?”

His mouth tightened.

“Mine.”

The word was not proud.

That mattered.

I wrote: dangerous offensive curse; created for use against enemies; capable of fatal blood loss; creator possesses counter-curse.

Snape read over my shoulder.

“Add that the counter-curse requires immediate application.”

I did.

“And that dittany alone is inadequate for severe wounds.”

I did.

He sat back.

“Anything else?”

“Yes.”

His eyes narrowed.

“Would you teach it now?”

The question changed the room.

“No.”

“Even to an Auror?”

“No.”

“A healer, so they could recognize it?”

He paused.

“The counter-curse, perhaps. Not the curse.”

“Why?”

“Because knowledge is not morally neutral simply because it is knowledge.”

I looked at him.

“That sounds like something you learned the hard way.”

His expression was dry. “Most durable lessons are.”

We worked down the list.

A charm that prevented ink from being read over one's shoulder.

A variation on a slicing charm that cut plant stems without bruising them.

A spell for keeping cauldron fumes from clinging to fabric.

I laughed at that one.

“What?”

“You invented a laundry charm.”

“It is a laboratory charm.”

“It keeps robes from smelling like boiled spleen.”

“It prevents contamination.”

“Laundry.”

“I regret telling you.”

“You're a domestic genius.”

“Stop.”

There was a charm that warmed boots from the inside.

I laughed harder.

Snape threatened to terminate the interview.

“Were you cold?” I asked.

His expression changed.

The humor left me at once.

Spinner's End.

Too-large clothes. Poor heating. A boy who knew magic existed but lived in a house where comfort was scarce.

“Sorry,” I said.

He looked down at the list.

“Yes,” he said.

One word.

No defensiveness.

I did not make it tragic.

I wrote utility warming charm and moved on.

By afternoon, the list had become something stranger than evidence.

It was a portrait of a mind.

Privacy spells.

Silencing spells.

Defensive counters.

Cruel jokes.

Efficient tools.

A brutal curse.

A warm-boot charm.

Nothing about Snape was ever only one thing.

The final spell on his list had no name.

“What does it do?”

He hesitated.

Then he lifted his wand and pointed at a cracked glass vial on the table.

The fracture sealed.

I examined it.

The repair was perfect.

“Reparo?”

“No. Reparo restores form. This restores certain magical tolerances in potion glass after curse exposure.”

“You invented it during the war?”

“Yes.”

“For the school?”

“Yes.”

“Why no name?”

“I had other concerns.”

I smiled faintly.

“What would you call it now?”

“I would not.”

“Everything deserves a name eventually.”

“An unsubstantiated claim.”

I tapped the parchment.

“We need something for the hearing.”

“Restitutio Vitri.”

“Glass restoration.”

“Accurate.”

“Boring.”

“Accuracy often is.”

I looked at the repaired vial.

“Not always.”

He caught the tone.

His eyes met mine.

I felt that now-familiar shift under my ribs.

The one I kept refusing to name.

Snape looked away.

“Submit the list,” he said.

“With restrictions.”

“Obviously.”

I smiled.

He noticed.

“Do not.”

“You said it.”

“It is a word.”

“It is your word.”

“I do not own vocabulary.”

“Half the castle would disagree.”

He reached for the flobberworm jar.

I moved the list out of range.

For enemies, I thought.

Once, he had written those words beside the cruelest thing he created.

Now he was choosing which knowledge to preserve, which to share, which to keep contained.

It was not redemption by paperwork.

Nothing was that simple.

But it was a choice.

And then another.

We spent the next hour sorting the spells into categories.

Useful. Reckless. Defensive. Cruel. Dependent on context. Never teach without supervision. Never teach at all.

Snape objected to my labels until I made him propose better ones.

He did.

Of course he did.

Muffliato went under controlled utility with a note about consent and privacy. Levicorpus earned a long argument because its original use had become tangled with schoolyard humiliation from more than one direction. Sectumsempra remained alone on the final page.

“What about a countercurse?” I asked.

His face sharpened.

“I know one.”

“Should other healers?”

He stared at the word for enemies on the copied page.

“Yes.”

The answer cost him something.

We drafted a sealed medical note describing the wound pattern and emergency response without including instructions for casting the curse itself.

“You realize,” I said, “this may save someone from a spell you invented.”

“I am aware.”

“That's not nothing.”

“No.” His quill paused. “Nor is it enough to make inventing it admirable.”

“I didn't say it was.”

His eyes met mine.

For once, we did not need to argue the difference.

And another.
